snippets.text: All right, everybody. We're laughing it up here. It's the All-In Podcast.
Apparently, slow news weeks continue. Once again, we struggle to put together a docket,
but we're going to try to get something together here, Sacks. I don't know what's in the news.
Maybe you have a SaaS corner for us. Any new hotness drop in the SaaS world or no?
Yeah, Benny L. rolled out a new reporting feature. I'm only top of docket material.
All right, that is top of docket. You're right. You're right. And Friedberg, of course, is here
cackling. He's in a good mood, but I understand you almost died in the last week. What were you,
in the hospital? You had to float? I got the pneumonia. Not good. Very bad. Very bad.
I do not wish it upon anyone. Knocked out in the hospital. Everyone, stay safe.
All right. Well, I saw everybody with their social media well-wishing you. And of course,
Chamath Palihapitiya is here, and it's a deep pull for Chamath today, a deep pull from the closet.
My Lord, I haven't seen that sweater since Biden was in office.
It's a nice ribbed cashmere mock turtleneck. Okay, ribbed for Chamath's pleasure.
Ribbed for Chamath's pleasure. All right, listen.
I thought it was supposed to be ribbed for her pleasure.
It's for her pleasure. But it's Chamath. It's all for Chamath's pleasure.
It's always for his pleasure.
Absolutely. That's who he is. All right, listen. Jensen is out as NVIDIA's CEO after an insane
series of events that happened in the past week. All of this played out in just six days,
starting Friday, November 6, and obviously record on Thursdays, which would be November 12.
Here's where things stand as of the taping of this episode.
NVIDIA's CFO will serve as the interim CEO. The board's looking for a new chief executive.
NVIDIA reports earnings next Tuesday, critical moment for the company,
and the stock has been crushed down 15% in the last week, which is hundreds of billions of dollars.
Here's the timeline that led to Jensen's ouster. Last Friday, November 6, right after the midterms,
interesting timing, the New York Times published a report claiming a Chinese businesswoman who had
a close relationship with Jensen was actually a CCP spy, a Chinese Communist Party spy.
The woman is named Alice Wang. No relation to Jensen. They just happened to share the same
last name. We'll call her Alice for the rest of this discussion. She's an executive at a Singapore
based company called Megaspie. They build data centers in Asia. They rent compute to companies,
including Chinese ones like Alibaba. According to the information, their relationship, Jensen's
analysis helped facilitate 7.5 billion in chips to Chinese companies since 2023. The New York Times
article was based on a leaked intelligence memo that identified Alice as a Chinese spy. No one
knows who leaked it. On Sunday, November 8, Jensen sent a company-wide email admitting he
had an affair and that the board would be investigating on Wednesday. The New York Times
reported Jensen had a second affair with a direct report. There's reports of a third
potential affair. Let's put all that aside and focus on his resignation, which came after 33 years
as CEO. Important caveat. This story has been hiding in plain sight for well over a year.
The New York Times first mentioned Alice's relationship with Jensen back in October 2025,
not this October 2026, 13 months ago. They published a follow-up last month,
Nvidia chief seen as target of Chinese spy plot. Culper Research, spelled C-U-L-P-E-R,
is a hedge fund that put a short on Nvidia, according to their tweetstorm, six months ago.
They published their thesis, which was based on Nvidia underselling its reliance on China
for chip sales. They even mentioned Megaspie by name in that tweetstorm, which you can see on
the screen right here. This is a disaster for the White House. There are reports of finger
pointing as officials try to figure out why Megaspie was left off the export control list
after these New York Times articles. And we'll get into more export control issues later.
Okay, Sacks, we're dealing with partial information here. This is a breaking news
story. Caveat, caveat, disclaimer, disclaimer. But let me ask you a simple question. Given
the New York Times reporting, what's your take on what they've released to date?
First of all, let me just say that I think this is a tragic situation. Okay, it's tragic for
Jensen and his family and for Nvidia and its employees. And I would say it's tragic
for the United States of America, because Jensen is one of the key reasons why we have
a major advantage in AI accelerator chips and GPUs. And that in turn is one of our key
advantages in the AI or super intelligence race. In fact, Jensen made such a good chip
that many people in Washington wanted to export control that. I think people kind of forget.
Jensen's been working on GPUs for over three decades. And he believed in this technology,
in this architecture, when everyone else was making CPUs, and his company almost went out
of business multiple times. It was his vision that created the GPU, which ended up being the key
chip that's used in AI. And it's the fact that Nvidia is so far ahead of everybody else, that
is what gives the United States a key advantage in this thing we call the AI or super intelligence
race. So I think this is a tragic situation. And I think that what's happened here is, I mean,
clearly, it's not a great situation for all the individuals involved. I don't think this
redoubts the benefit of the United States either. And it's very unfortunate that this whole
situation could not have been resolved in a different way. Now, let's talk about the story
that's come out. I think it's pretty clear that there were two ops here. So one op is whatever
Alice Wong was doing with or without the Chinese Communist Party. There may have been smuggling
involved. We don't know there is an investigation going on. And there should be an investigation.
We should get all the facts there. We've talked on this podcast about how we do not believe that
leading edge chips should go to China. And if there's any smuggling going on that that is
wrong. And that it should be stopped. The government should crack down on that. So that
investigation should continue. We should get all the facts there. And we should find out what
actually happened. So that is one op is whatever Alice Wong was doing, again, with or without
the CCP. But however, there's also a second op here. And that second op began when somebody
or multiple people leaked a highly classified memo or the consents of it to the New York Times.
I think it's really important to understand that that's a crime. I mean, leaking classified
intelligence is a crime and many people have been prosecuted for it. In fact, we had
multiple former presidents and current presidents, President Trump and President Biden, their homes
were raided because supposedly they had classified documents in their possession.
Remember that there was a raid on Mar-a-Lago, there was a raid on Joe Biden's garage and they
found the box. This happens to everybody, it seems. Yeah. Well, I don't know if it
happens to everybody, but it's a serious crime. And, you know, because of that fact,
I don't believe that the New York Times just got this by overhearing people talking about
it at a bar. Somebody made the calculated decision that they're willing to risk going
to jail, they're willing to risk committing a crime to let the New York Times know about this
story. And so I have a series of questions about that. So number one is first, who did that and
why? What was their motivation? Why did they feel so strongly about taking Jensen down that had to
be at least a part of their motive that they're willing to break the law? And I do think it makes
sense for there to be an investigation opened into this leak as there have been with many other
classified leaks. I don't know why there hasn't been an investigation open as far as we know
into this. So that would be question number one is why this leak. And the New York Times has given
a clue there. Obviously, Rubio was leading this investigation, briefed President Trump on it,
and the New York Times attributed the story, the spy part of the story anonymously to quote,
people briefed on the surveillance. Yes, but just let's be very clear here. I don't,
I don't really like you using Marco Rubio's name there, but because he's a national security
advisor. If there was a classified memo, then obviously it would be done under his
revision as the head of the NSC. Yeah, I'm not insinuating he's the leak, but it's somebody he may
have briefed. Okay, when the New York Times says people briefed on the matter, that is an extremely
vague and broad terminology. And it could be very low level officials who did this. And when the
New York Times even uses the word official, that doesn't mean they're a senior person in an
administration. They could be very, very low level. And it could also be the case that their
careers, which is to say non-political appointees, that just because they're serving in the executive
branch of the Trump administration doesn't mean that they are Trump officials. So look,
we don't know who committed the leak. All we know is they committed a crime. And I do think
that we should be asking the question, who did that and why? Okay, so that's sort of bucket
number one of questions. Bucket number two is around the failure to give the defensive briefing.
If the national security state is worried that Jensen is in possession of national security
secrets and might leak them to someone who they suspect is a spy, why wouldn't you go to him right
away and tell him, hey, you have this problem, don't talk to this person. Apparently that didn't
happen. And it does sound like that is some sort of standard operating procedure. Let me give you
an example. So we have the case of Eric Swalwell. Okay, so Eric Swalwell was a congressman. He was on
the House Intelligence Committee. It eventually came out and I believe it was the finding of an
investigation that he had a personal relationship with a Chinese spy. Fang Fang is the story.
Yes, the New York Post memorably memorialized this with its cover called Fang Fang Bang Bang.
You know, it was the story that came out. What was the Democrats reaction to that?
They gave him a defensive briefing. He said he cut off the relationship and they allowed him to stay
in Congress. He certainly did not have to resign. And in fact, he didn't even resign
from the Intelligence Committee. So they allowed him to keep not only a seat in Congress,
but his seat on the Intelligence Committee. So obviously in this, I'd say very high profile
example, people did not think it was necessary to resign. They thought that what it was necessary
to do is to let the person know, allow them to cut off contact, and then you'd be able to move
on from there. So this situation was handled very differently. Okay, that brings me to
question number three, which is what exactly were the national security secrets that Jensen
supposedly knew? He doesn't work for the government. He's not, as far as I'm aware,
privy to classified materials. So what is it that people say that he leaked to this suspected
intelligence asset that's never been explained? I just have that question. What I can say is that,
you know, as the CEO of Silicon Valley technology company, Silicon Valley tech companies are very
open about their plans or product development plans, things like that. Is there IP that the
CCP would like to get a hold of? I'm sure. But to be blunt, it's not the type of IP that you're
going to convey over pillow talk. It would be things like files that would allow you to tape
out the next generation of chips. That's the kind of thing where frankly, if the ministry
of state security or whoever is spying for the Chinese wanted to get ahold of that stuff,
I think you'd much rather have a line engineer who can go into Nvidia, find the relevant files and
extract them somehow maybe on a thumb drive, or you do a cyber attack and you get the files that
way. That would make a lot more sense to me as the way to basically get ahold of,
you know, let's say secrets. Now, I see some people saying that, well,
Nvidia makes a product that is subject to export controls, therefore, that's a national
security product, therefore, national security secrets. Okay, that is a very broad misleading
hand wave over the situation. I can go out and buy a Blackwell chip as an American. None of us are
restricted from doing that. Certain foreign countries are restricted from doing that,
but we're not. And if we buy a Blackwell chip and run it in our own little server rack,
we are not in possession of national security secrets. You cannot reverse engineer the design of
a chip by getting ahold of the wafer. It doesn't work that way. You have to get the files.
Those chips can, of course, help you make cutting edge LLMs like the ones they've been delivering.
Okay, I understand, but that's not what we're talking about right now. Okay, we're talking about
the question that I have is what secrets are we talking about that just supposedly compromise?
The last question I have, and then I'll stop, is what is the evidence that this person,
Alice Wong, was actually a Chinese spy who worked for the Ministry of State Security?
And here's what I think is quite unusual. Just this morning, there was an article that came out
in Politico where the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, who's a Democrat,
he came out of a classified briefing on this subject. And in the hallway with this fresh in
his mind, he came out and said that he's not sure that this person is a Chinese spy. He said
she might be a useful idiot. Okay, well, now what is a useful idiot? A useful idiot is someone who
doesn't work for the Chinese government is not a spy. It's just that maybe somehow they're being
taken advantage of. Okay, so look, I have a set of questions about this. So let's put this all
together. Okay, there's two ops here. There's whatever Alice Wong was doing, that potential
smuggling operation, it should be figured out. There's a second op that I think also needs to
be investigated and figured out. And the components of that are one, who leaked this
classified material in violation of the law? That's the only crime to date that we even know about.
Number two, why wasn't Jensen given a defensive briefing, which is standard operating procedure. It
was done with Eric Swalwell. Number three, what secrets is Jensen accused of leaking? What
secrets would even be in his possession? And number four, was Alice Wong even a Chinese spy,
because now the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, who's a Democrat,
just threw major cold water on that. So I put all these things together. And I would say at
this point in time, I think there's more questions than answers. Yes. And I would like,
I would like a full accounting of the facts to come out. There's a fifth question though,
to your Sacks, which is why at all and why now? Meaning like, why did whoever pulled the pin on
this grenade, what did they see where they felt this had to happen? And then why now?
And the other discrediting affair stories coming out in a coordinated way at the same time,
like it all happens at once. What is the motivation?
Probably, and I'm just speculating here, but I'm not the only one who has looked at this.
You had China Hawks who lost this debate about sending chip technology to China from the United
States. And they want to reverse that and they want to have no chips sent to China. And they
also want to put GPS and other ways of tracking these chips and back during them in order to
turn them off. Something that Jensen has been opposed to something a number of senators have
been pro doing. So there could be a contingent in the White House who are very anti-China,
who want to see the policy with China change Friedberg.
Yeah. So that's one. The bigger longer term picture, which I've mentioned several times,
there's two paths for the future, I would argue. One is a path where AI technology is broadly
accessible, broadly used, and the value of it is not concentrated. And the power of it
is not concentrated in the hands of a few and controlled by a few. Where open source AI
distributed data centers that are available and accessible to many, gives everyone the ability
to use AI to rise up, to progress, to create value, and so on. That is a scary and threatening
thing because of how it changes a lot of power structures, economic structures, and so on.
It creates a lot of instability in existing social, economic, and political systems. So the
alternative path for the world is one of concentrated power and influence over AI technology.
This is where I've had this theory that ultimately data centers will get regulated,
but maybe further down the stack here with chips becomes the point of control. But
fundamentally, there's a motivation to not lose control and to not let the power structures
that exist in the world today get diminished by AI. And so we could argue there's probably a broad
set of interests there that start to say, hey, this guy's not aligned, Jensen's not aligned with
our view of the world. Jensen has been a strong advocate for open source. He's been a strong
advocate for global access to and utilization of AI technology for the benefit of humanity,
not just for the benefit of American citizens. And those views are counter to perhaps a lot
of different interested parties. And clearly, there was knowledge about this woman, about Jensen's
other relationships or whatever is coming out that's being used to smear him a long time ago.
And to Chamath's point, this is a moment where it's all coming out at once. And in such a
way that it almost guaranteed that he would be ousted. And I'll just highlight Jensen being
ousted is you've got to ask the question, what is the fiduciary duty of the board?
What do they actually have a responsibility to act on? And the one thing they have a responsibility
to act on is if Jensen lied. Obviously, if he committed espionage or did something that's
criminal, and he would have been arrested, right? Yeah. So if there's something criminal,
violation of federal law, that is obviously, you know, they have to act on that you have
to terminate him. And clearly, because there wasn't an arrest or something like that,
it doesn't seem like that's, I think we can take that off the table, right? So perhaps
the next likely thing is that he actually made a misrepresentation about something. So, you know,
companies have what's called a code of conduct in the code of conduct, it says you have to
report relationships, you have to report relationships with subordinates, you cannot
have a personal conflict of interest with a customer, or a partner, a key business partner
without reporting it. And executives or section 16 officers at public companies have to make
quarterly attestations that they are in an auditable way, not in violation of the
code of conduct that things are auditable. And that attestation might be what gets him in
trouble ultimately, where he made attestations that said, I am not violating any of our code of
conduct, I am not in violation of any of our business practices, which would include not having
conflicting personal relationships with customers or partners, that may be what gets him tricked up.
So fundamentally, I think the board action isn't related necessarily to the
the personal relationships, but there's something else that's going on here,
that ultimately, he probably looked at and said, Hey, you know, we should probably fast track
through this. And it is extraordinarily sad and disappointing. This is a man who worked at Denny's.
And in 1993, started a chip company that no one believed in that everyone thought was a feature,
not a platform, not a product, not much of a business. And the stock price was, you know,
pennies, compared to the price today, it was less than $2 a share 10 years ago, 100.
They're making video game cards and servicing the Bitcoin.
From 2006 to 2016, the stock price did not move 10 years of just being a nothing company with a
$12 billion market cap. Think about that you start this company in 93. And in 2006, it's worth 10,
12 billion bucks, and it doesn't move for 10 years. And you're grinding and you're grinding.
And this is your whole life, your whole business, everything and you believe and you see this
vision and you just keep going and you compound and you build a moat and you compound and you
build a moat and you compound and you get an amazingly talented team. And all of a sudden,
four years ago, this thing starts to take off in 20Xs in the last four years and is the most valuable
company on earth delivering the most profitable quarter in business history, $63 billion in
operating profit more than any other company ever. And then all of a sudden, boom, he gets taken out.
I mean, you know, it is disheartening. And I think that obviously, there's something that
was done wrong. And we're going to find out and I'm not going to rush to judgment. I'm not
going to rush to diminish whatever he did that was wrong. But there's a sad arc to this whole story.
And there's something very fundamental, I think, to the power structure that is being
rewritten in the world today with AI to the story. Okay, Chamath, let me ask you, Qibono,
Qimalo, who benefits and who is harmed by Jensen being taken out of that seat? Let's assume
he's not a traitor. I find that absurd and insane based on just what we've seen over these
past couple of decades and his effort and his character. Okay, he's got some personal things
going on. But who is the beneficiary of Jensen being removed as CEO? Who benefits from that?
Let me just pile on first before I give you my thoughts. I also think he's an incredible
individual and CEO. And he's built the industry that will reshape our entire lives, our children's
lives and our children's children's lives. I think in a decade or two, when you see solutions to
diseases and cancers, and we have this abundance that we were told is coming, he will have been as
instrumental as anyone, if not more than anybody. Okay, so that's the tragedy of what happened is
a person that was an architect of something this grand was defenestrated this unceremoniously.
Very tactically, I think Friedberg really nailed it around what probably happened at the board
level that led to his resignation. When you are an officer of a company, and when you file your 10
k's, every quarter, you have to get on the phone with your auditor. And you have to go through
these sets of questions that they ask you. And they ask you these exact things, you know, do you
have a conflict with someone? Are you in a relationship with someone, etc, etc. Now, why do
those things happen? The SEC requires that to make sure that you're not running afoul of any
conflict of interest so that your company is a reliable steward of capital on behalf of the
shareholders. But even more tactically, you need that for things like DNO insurance, which is
like the director and officer insurance, which is what gives a wrapper of liability.
For board members and for officers to do the job of running public companies. And there are covenants
associated with all of these things. And so when you get into a situation where you may have
misrepresented something and you start to breach covenants, those are the actual dominoes that tip
it may not be nearly as salacious as what people want to believe is happening at the board.
But those are the tactics of the boardroom discussions. They're extremely tactical,
sadly, which is again why it's even more tragic when you compare that to, you know, what he is,
which is this giant. Okay, so who benefits Jason? I think there's a lot of people that have rushed
to this conclusion that China wins. And I would just try to unpack that and ask the question,
is that true? So let's take two cases. And these are both hypothetical to sort of try to
answer this question. Let's say that there are no chips going to China. Well, why does China
win? No chips were going before. No chips are going to go now. China is stuck in the same place that
they were before, which is they need an endemic solution that can replace the compute capability
of NVIDIA. Even without Jensen there, there's still years and years and years, maybe
potentially decades, and hundreds of thousands of man hours of work that NVIDIA has put into
building the moat that they built that doesn't get overcome just because he's not there anymore.
So maybe China can catch up. But I still think that that's a multi year potentially multi decade
endeavor. Now let's assume the other side, hypothetically, let's say that the chips were
somehow leaking into the hands of the Chinese, maybe not into China, but into the hands of the
Chinese. Well, it looks like the government's going to crack down and figure out where every chip went.
And so presumably now they're not getting the chips. So whatever they were doing, they're now
going to be held back, which is to say that whatever progress they were making has gotten
taken away. So that's a disadvantage to China. So as I think about it, in both scenarios,
China is sort of where they were or worse off. So I don't think that they benefit.
What about NVIDIA's competitors? Does this help AMD or Google or startups,
Cerebrus or Etched or whomever? And my answer there is, again, not really. Why? Because
those companies need something very different, which is they need to spend an enormous amount
of time still making their chips work at scale. And then convincing folks like TSMC and
others, Samsung, to give them manufacturing capacity, HBM capacity, etc. And as we've
learned the hard way, you can't just will your way to a training run of a million GPUs
that just works. This has again been many, many hours of work. So they don't necessarily
benefit in the short term. They still have a lot of work that they have to do.
The only cohort of people that I think has the potential to win are those that want some
version of what Friedberg said, which is a more centralized governance infrastructure of compute
capacity. And very narrowly, what I would say is, right now, when you export chips,
what they ask of the exporter is have telemetry, right? We need to know when and how the chips
are being used, and we need to have a remote kill switch. But that is a private responsibility
that's born through the regulatory infrastructure. Amazon has to have that, Microsoft has to have
that, Google has to have that. There is a version of this where now, if we think that
it's been leaking, and there hasn't been enough checks and balances, there is an opening for
certain individuals in the government to propose telemetry and a kill switch that is
owned by them. Now, narrowly, they would win now in this scenario, because if they were
looking for control before, they've now been given an opening to ask for the legislation to get it.
So I'm kind of at a loss. I don't think that the takes right now that I've seen on X
really track for me. I think this is the one narrow take that I believe where there's a clear
advantage, everybody else just still has an enormous amount of work to do. It has not changed
their homework. Jason, what's your take on all of this?
Yeah, so I've been thinking about it from two vectors. The first is, you know, who should
make the decision that Jensen's out? Obviously, I think it's the shareholders. And if you look at
the investigation, it's not complete, I think they should have waited till it's complete,
and the press and the mobs and all of this shouldn't make too much of an impact on that.
He did agree to resign himself, obviously, under a lot of pressure. There is something about
governance here that we need to consider, which is the people who are on the board who are making
this decision are doing it from a CYA position, cover their butts, and they're not doing it,
I think, in the best interest of the shareholders. And they don't own a meaningful
percentage of the share. So I think this should be put to a shareholder vote if what
we're seeing here is not Jensen doing something criminal. And it still hasn't been proven,
as you pointed out, Sacks, who this person was and what their motivation was, are they a spy,
or are they just somebody trying to make money? It's unclear for me, or at least from the data
we've seen what's going on there. Now, on the question that we've been discussing of who benefits
from this, and it's really who benefits from America's champion in super intelligence,
you know, getting angled, because this could have a lot of impact on NVIDIA and then America's lead.
And so the partners, the employees, the shareholders, they're all losers here. So
who's the leaker of this document? It can't be the competitors. It's not the shareholders,
obviously, and I don't think it's China. And then that leaves, I think, maybe the people who are
the D cells here. And that also seems a bit farcical that entropic or the D cells would try to
consolidate power on this because they need the chips as well. And I think that's where I think,
my personal opinion, that there's something going on in the White House, in the administration,
between warring factions of who wants China to get no chips, the China Hawks, and maybe the
people who want to maybe cool off the relationship with China and make it more productive.
I think at the end of the day, we're going to find the leak is coming from within the house. That's
my belief. There's also a chance it could be a Democrat who is a D cell and who wants to damage
the White House just completely. Because why did they let not inform Jensen to Hillary Clinton's
point? Maybe it's just somebody on the Democratic side who wants to cause chaos. I'm speculating
here in a massive way. Just taking a broader view on the role that NVIDIA is playing currently,
it may not just be about chips to China, but it may actually be about slowing down
the US AI economy. Because remember, NVIDIA is actually providing capital and guarantees
to startups, to data centers, to a lot of infrastructure. A lot of that is directed
directly by Jensen. Chamath, you're pretty close to this, but if Jensen's out of the picture,
is there someone in NVIDIA that continues running that effort? That's potentially hundreds
of billions of dollars of capital that gets turned off that's flowing to the AI economy.
I think Collette Kress and the head of M&A and corp. Dev Vishal Bhagwani, these guys are
really smart, good guys, but you are kind of right. The Bank of NVIDIA ran through Jensen.
It's not clear what happens now. Is the bank closed indefinitely? Is it closed for
some period of time and it restarts? Will the new CEO feel the latitude to invest as aggressively?
I think Jensen had a much more holistic view of the industry. He knew how to move
the chips around on the board and he had the moral authority to make investments and to make
acquisitions that will probably be harder for a more traditional CEO who will have to have
committees and analyses and a level of diligence that will just slow things down at best.
Totally. And he has a sense for it. He intuits the whole thing. He knows the market. He knows
where things are going. He knows the people personally with him out of the picture.
And he's lived it, so he has mastery.
He's like the beating heart of the AI economy and all of a sudden...
I think it's beyond obvious. You asked the question, Kweebona, who benefits? It's China.
China benefits from this because Jensen is a tentpole of our entire AI ecosystem.
I mean, that's the bottom line. Now, do I think that China leaked this and took Jensen down?
Well, I think we know the answer to that is no, because the New York Times has described its
sources as people who got briefed on this intelligence. So they're either in the government
or one degree away from it. So again, the proximate cause of the leak here was this
classified memo. So the rational thing would be that China did take him down, but I think we
know that this was domestic and it comes down to the fact that Jensen made powerful enemies,
either as a result of his policies or because of his company's success. And some of those people
eventually took him down.
Wait, you're saying Jensen made enemies of certain people in America?
Guys, this is not in doubt. The New York Times says who... They described their source very
broadly, but it's people who were briefed on the classified memo. That's not someone from the CCP.
Well, obviously not, if that's true within the New York Times.
But you asked the question in whose interest is this? In a narrow sense,
obviously, Nvidia's competitors, in a broader sense, China. They're the ones who benefit.
But look, I don't think we should speculate about that too much. This is one of those
areas where we just don't have the facts yet. I think it's an area where, frankly,
they should try to get the facts. I mean, again, the only crime that we know was committed for sure
in all of this was the leaking of that classified memo. So it would be nice if there was an
